paper.title_en: Femtosecond Free-Space Time-Frequency Transfer at km/s Relative Motion with Doppler Compensation
paper.abstract_en: A global optical clock network holds great promise for a wide range of applications, including international metrology--particularly the redefinition of the ``second''--as well as navigation, geoscience, and fundamental physics. Satellite-based high-precision time-frequency dissemination is essential for realizing such a network. Despite remarkable progress in ground-based free-space simulations over high-loss channels, the Doppler effect arising from satellite motion has remained an unsolved barrier. Here we demonstrate femtosecond two-way time-frequency transfer over a 113-km free-space link under simulated Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s. To overcome the Doppler barrier, we first reproduce satellite-like Doppler shifts of up to 1.55 km/s on the ground by locking a frequency comb to a broadly tunable laser. We then correct the resulting disturbances with two complementary techniques: a dual-channel sampling architecture that compensates for optical dispersion and radio frequency (RF) nonlinearity while eliminating Nyquist dead zones, and an iterative interferogram reconstruction algorithm that removes Doppler-induced distortion. After correction, residual systematic errors are within $\pm10$ fs over the full 1.55 km/s range. Using simulated medium earth orbit (MEO) and geosynchronous orbit (GSO) satellite trajectories, we achieve fractional frequency instability of $3.9\times10^{-19}$ at 4,600 s and $3.6\times10^{-19}$ at 23,600 s, respectively. This extends the operational velocity range by nearly two orders of magnitude beyond previous free-space demonstrations, removing the last major technical barrier to a global femtosecond-precision satellite-based time-frequency link.
